summary: Read voiced-teachings notes 0..749 (750 notes, 49 games; phases 304 opening / 295 middlegame / 151 endgame). The reference coach talks on every move but the volume is tiered: about 200 of 750 notes are under 12 words (a bare narration of a forced or routine move), about 17 are 80+ word lectures (a whole plan or a whole recovery method dumped at one decision point), and the rest are one or two sentences that pair the move with ONE reason. His signature acts, ranked by how often they appear: (1) naming the opening/structure on arrival (~95 notes) and the plan it implies; (2) "not X, but Y, because Z": rejecting the natural or tempting alternative before naming the move (~49 'rather than/instead' notes, ~49 'because/the point'); (3) the drawback or the squares a move abandons (~30); (4) prevention and prophylaxis, stopping a pin, a b5 kick or a lever before it happens (~30); (5) the consequence played as an if-then line (~30 'if they…'); (6) pins, x-rays and batteries (~67 mentions); (7) "first this, then that" move-order reasoning (~35); (8) rule plus its exception (f6 is bad unless it hits something; a rim knight is fine as a layover; you may break a principle only once you know it); (9) targets and weaknesses: the weakness's worth is the defenders it ties down; (10) traps and tricks in the opening (~18), stated as the trap the move sets or sidesteps (the centre-fork trick, Bg4 pin into d4); (11) endgame technique nuggets (attack a pawn from behind, defend a pawn with a pawn, freeze a pawn along its rank, queen against a seventh-rank pawn won by zugzwang, pawn breakthrough, keep checking and the mate arrives); (12) method/habit lines (define the concrete threat before reacting; the three answers to a check; when the king is weak start with captures beside it; re-read the plan after every enemy move; know which decisions matter so you don't burn the clock). Most acts already have a computer: refutedAlternative, deliberation, thinkAloud.notYet, ruleException, theirMoveCost, moveInsight.weakenedBy / theirMoveChanged / pawnHook / fileToOpen, forkTrick, latentDanger, pinGeometry / pinPressure, exchangeLedger / countMethod, recaptureChoice, tempoCount, outpost, planRace, endgamePawnReads, conversionMethod, conceptEngine, zugzwang, queenVsPawn, checkMethod, methodBeat, openingIdentity / openingAnnouncement, theoryDeparture, amateurPlayLookup, speedRunReads. Genuinely MISSING: a prophylaxis computer (what the opponent wants next and the quiet move that removes it, e.g. h3 against Bg4, a4 against b5, Kh2 against Nf4/sac on h3); a move-order computer ("e6 first BECAUSE it opens Bd6, which then guards e5"); a transposition / independent-value computer ("this move has no life of its own, it transposes"); a "what this setup buys you in move-order" computer (one setup against everything); a decision-importance-for-the-clock line (it has criticality numbers but no time-management habit sentence); a self-evaluation exercise ("list the factors, guess the number"); and a weakness-ties-defenders read (pressure on a defended point still pays because the guard can't leave), which exists only as prose in boardConcepts/moveInsight and not as a computed fact. Two things the reference coach does that we must NOT copy: thinking out loud with uncertainty or admitting he missed something (7 notes; F18 says the coach always knows the answer), and narrating his own blitz history or opponents' behaviour ("they pre-moved"). The name never appears in this report.
rhythm: The opening is dense and personal. Almost every move gets a full clause: the opening's name, what the move prepares or stops, the trap it sets or dodges, and often the sideline the student might face ("the main move is X, but Y is the reputable alternative"). Several points on one move are normal, and a quiet-looking move (c3, h3, Be2 instead of Nf3) gets the most words, because it hides the idea or the trap. At the opening's end there is often ONE long plan paragraph that lays out the whole middlegame road (break, lever, which file, where each piece goes). The middlegame swings between short clauses on forced moves and a full deliberation at decision points: the tempting move, why it fails, the move, and the line if they answer it. Recaptures, retreats and forced replies get 3-8 words. The endgame drops to terse narration ("king to g1", "you take back") with a technique nugget every few moves and a closing line on the conversion method (double on the seventh, keep checking, push the passer). Concretely, in notes 0..749: ~27% under 12 words, ~2% over 80 words, and the rest one or two sentences. The long ones cluster at (a) the end of the opening, where the plan is laid out, (b) a critical defensive moment (list the threats, then the one move that covers both), and (c) a recovery/method lecture when the position is lost. Nothing passes in silence: routine moves are still voiced, just briefly. That is V11 plus V19 in practice.

summary:
Read notes[750..1499] of public/data/voiced-teachings.json (750 notes, 37 videos; 327 opening / 316 middlegame / 107 endgame). Only 56 carry a `teaches` field, 6 a `plans` field, 0 carry `concepts`, so the teaching lives in the `explains` prose. I sorted it into 34 distinct teaching acts below. Most already have a computer in src/services that could produce them; the real gaps are listed as MISSING.

How the reference coach teaches, in short:
- **Opening moves.** He names the opening or system and says why it exists. He gives the move's job (what it prepares, what it stops), its drawback, and the tempting move with why it fails. He picks a branch at a crossroads, and he warns about the trap around the move (the centre fork trick, Bxf7+ ideas, the stock pattern that fails here).
- **Middlegame.** He reads the structure (chain base, levers, holes, bad bishops). He judges every trade and every recapture, counts attackers against defenders, and scans for loose pieces and x-rays. He says the consequence as a line played out in words, all the way to mate or material. He states the long plan as numbered steps, and keeps referring back to standing plans.
- **Endgame.** King first and centralise, make the passer, simplify when ahead, push rather than defend, and stay alert to counterplay to the end.
- **Habits.** He closes on the habit: "always look at the undefended pieces and x-rays", "catalog their weaknesses", "make every threat meaningful".

Missing computers, in priority order:
1. Pin broken with tempo: the pinned piece leaves with check (notes 1040, 1404). This matches brief item 7.
2. The stock pattern that fails here: the familiar tactic that loses because of one counter-move (1027-1031).
3. A threat must be meaningful, not just hit the queen (1396).
4. Delay committing a piece until the opponent shows where theirs go (1113).
5. Opposite-side castling: attack with pieces, and pawn storms are often overrated (879-881, 1434).
6. The hook pawn a storm opens against (1434-1436).
7. A piece is only truly safe when a pawn defends it (1313).
8. Give up the exchange to keep the piece that delivers the attack (1146).
9. Fix the enemy pawns on your bishop's colour (1126).
10. Pressure piled on a point forces resources there, with a standing sacrifice threat (1133).
11. "Top priority" framing: save the vulnerable piece before anything else (1492).
12. One setup against every system: let them declare (1050, 1041).
13. Opening history, like when a line first appeared (1245). openingIdentity.ts gives purpose, not history.
14. King safe in a closed centre, so no need to castle (1087, 1134, 1447). This is the inverse of the central-king-danger read.

Rule flags for David:
- **F0d.** The notes are full of first-person career claims: a line "I played against" a famous GM, "I learned this from" a famous world champion's game, "my old over-the-board line", a well-known course "I learned the move" from. They also name the live opponent several times (notes 862-883), name a player's "question" (1271), and shout out another streamer (1416). If any of this is spliced verbatim it breaks F0d. Two service files are named after the reference coach (danyaBehaviors.ts, danyaTeachingService.ts). They don't ship as text, but they show where his voice was copied.
- **F05.** Questions to the audience ("who can explain why…", 1118) would breach F05 except for a long-standing weakness in the student's record.
- **Rating advice.** "For players in this range…" (1111) must come from the student's record, not their rating.
- **Data.** Many consecutive notes are fragments of one spoken sentence split across plies (791-796, 1033-1039, 1381-1382, 1462-1466). Treat them as one thought, not per-ply prose.
rhythm:
How much he says depends on the moment, not the phase. Measured over notes 750-1499 (`explains` word counts):
- **Opening:** median 18 words, mean 30; 76 of 327 notes are 8 words or fewer, 19 are 60 or more.
- **Middlegame:** median 18.5, mean 23; 68 short, 20 long.
- **Endgame:** median 13, mean 16; 34 of 107 short, only 1 long.

The shape:
- Opponent replies and routine developing moves get a bare clause, often just the move ("White castles", "c4.").
- Each opening move he plays gets a purpose clause plus one more point: what it prepares, what it stops, or its drawback.
- Opening crossroads and tabias get a paragraph: the menu of replies with popularity, which branch he picks and why, and the trap around it.
- The middlegame turning point (where to put a piece, whether to trade, the sacrifice) gets the longest speech, 100 to 900 words. He thinks out loud: candidate, why not, the line in words, the habit.
- The endgame shrinks to directives ("king first", "simplify", "push it") plus counterplay checks.

Whole replayed games told without commentary (notes 964-1020) are bare move lists, which breaks V11's spirit of a short clause on every move.

Several points on one opening move is normal (898, 1188, 1329), which matches V19.

rhythm: Opening, to the hilt: about one to three reasons per move, plus the opening's name and history, which moves are main lines or sidelines, what players at the student's level usually play, and the punishment for each deviation. A single move can carry several points (note 1614: f3 stops a knight jump AND braces the centre). Middlegame, quiet then burst: short clauses on routine moves, then a long weighing paragraph at decision points (candidates, the drawback of each, the plan, the hidden tactic, and "what if I do it anyway"). Notes 1804 and 2249 are each over 150 words on ONE move. Endgame, mostly terse: move calls plus occasional nuggets (two connected passers too far from the enemy king; leave the opponent pawn moves so there is no stalemate; push one passer to deflect the rook, then queen the other). About 22% of this slice is bare move narration with no teaching. Our coach should not copy that silence-in-words; V11 requires at least a short clause on every move.

summary:
Read all 750 notes in public/data/voiced-teachings.json [2250..2999] (430 opening, 270 middlegame, 50 endgame; every note's `concepts` array is empty, so the tags gave nothing and the teaching had to be read out of the prose). Repo: /home/user/wt-work. Read-only throughout.

I found 33 distinct teaching acts in this slice. Most of them already have a computer behind them: speedRunReads.ts holds about 22 small checks, plus moveOrder.ts:65, recaptureChoice.ts:103, ruleException.ts:70, falseAlarm.ts:37, bluffDetector.ts:37, countMethod.ts:17, deliberation.ts:144, thinkAloud.ts (notYet :145, opponentHabits :180), concessionBeat.findStudentDrawback :360, theirMoveCost.ts:60, pinGeometry.pinBites :178, endgameTechnique.ts and matePatterns.ts. These all exist. Whether they actually reach the student is the census's question, not this one.

The clear gaps are:
- **Accessible-target test:** whether a weak pawn can actually be reached and attacked. Doubled or isolated pawns are a weakness only if they can be attacked, and a weak SQUARE stays weak after a pawn move covers the PAWN.
- **Exact transposition:** naming a position as a known opening with extra moves thrown in, or the same opening with colours reversed and a move up.
- **Gambit handling:** accept the pawn, then give it back to get ahead in development.
- **Pawn-storm function:** what the storm is for (dislodge the defending knight, open a file, win squares) and how a pawn hook lets it open lines.
- **Mate method:** take away the escape square first, then mate; clear the last defender with check; the promotion square is also the mating square.
- **Endgame conversion:** sacrifice the extra pawn as a decoy to reach a won pawn ending; stop grabbing pawns and convert, because each extra pawn matters less than the last.
- **Two-front principle:** open a second weakness before cashing the first.
- **Rarity of a good move:** "few players under 2000 find this".
- **The pawn thought experiment:** "if you could remove one of your own pawns, which would it be?"

Partial gaps:
- **Purpose/drawback tied to the punishing reply:** "this move leaves the bishop stuck, so the punishing reply is X" (theirMoveCost is close).
- **Pin judged by convenience:** "you can take on that pin whenever you like".
- **Hole timing:** a hole exists, but occupying it now is too early.

**Rhythm.**
- **Opening:** two modes. In plain book lines almost every move gets a short clause naming the move, its purpose and the line's name. Wherever the opponent leaves theory or a choice arises, there are several sentences on one move: what it prepares, what it stops, what it costs, the trap around it, and the reply that punishes it.
- **Middlegame:** short clauses during manoeuvring, then one long monologue at the decision moment. That monologue lists the candidate moves, rules out the tempting ones with their refutations, and plays the chosen line out to the result.
- **Endgame:** terse statements of technique, and the mate is named when it lands.
- **Ending a moment:** he usually closes on the habit or principle that would find the move next time.

This corpus is also an authoring source with a flaw to clean up: some `explains` entries in this slice carry the creator's first person ("my coach's line", "I like", "I didn't see"), named people, and a stray typo ("the onemy whole life"). V1 and F0d say these must never ship as they are.
rhythm: Opening (57% of the slice): the default is one clause per move: the move, its job, and the line's name. Examples of that shape: c3 in the Ruy is a retreat square plus prep for d4; h3 in the London keeps h2 for the bishop. It goes to the hilt, with three to six points on one move, at three triggers: an opponent's deviation or inaccuracy; a crossroads ("four worthy options here"); and a known trap. At those moments he says what the move costs, what punishes it, why the obvious punishment fails, and the reply to choose. Middlegame (36%): terse narration while pieces are manoeuvred, then one long monologue at the critical moment. The monologue weighs candidates, refutes the tempting one with its line, plays the line out to the material or mate result, and ends on a principle. Endgame (7%): short technical statements of rule and method; names the mate when it lands; often closes with a short recap of the game. Questions to the student ("what does d6 prepare?", "what's g4's function?") come before the answer at roughly one note in fifteen, always followed by the answer.

summary: Notes 3000–3749 of public/data/voiced-teachings.json come from 43 videos: 394 opening notes, 297 middlegame, 59 endgame. Only 68 have a `teaches` field and 5 have `plans`, so the teaching is in `explains`. The reference coach keeps doing four things. (1) He names what the move IS: the opening, the variation, its reputation and the level it is good for. (2) He weighs the choices out loud: the tempting move, why it fails, then the move he likes. (3) He states consequences as if-then lines with a reason. (4) He gives a portable principle or nugget, and he ranks principles against each other, for example that wrecking the king's shelter matters more than pawn structure in general (3212, 3356). Keyword counts over all 750 notes: king or castling 173, piece geometry (x-ray, diagonal, file, fork, pin, overload, discovery) 131, an evaluation word 70, move order or 'first' 64, if-then consequence 64, opening naming or theory 59, trap or blunder 57, a question put to the student 55, plan or reroute 50, principle 42, drawback 40, practical or human factor 37, structure 35, tempting-then-refuted 24, explicit attacker/defender counting only 5. Most teaching acts already have a computer: refutedAlternative / readWrongTry / buildDeliberation (weighing), findStudentDrawback (drawbacks), latentFork / pinGeometry / detectTactics (geometry and traps), exchangeChain / computeExchangeLedger (counting), kingSafety, tempoCount, planRace, openingIdentity, theoryDeparture, methodBeat (habits). MISSING: the question put to the student, move-order equivalence, 'this piece has done its job, reroute it', the ranking of one principle against another, human factors (clock, opponent level, betting on a slip), endgame conversion technique as one computer, and stating what a quiet opening move prepares, stops or allows (V19). In the opening he often says only the move and the opening's name; the full reasoning arrives at real decision points.
rhythm: Measured on notes 3000-3749 (median words in `explains`): opening 18 words, middlegame 27, endgame 15. By ply: plies 0-9 median 14; plies 10-29 median 28-30 (the peak, where the first real choices and tactics appear); plies 30-39 median 23; plies 40+ median 16, and 8 by ply 60+. 89 of 394 opening notes are 8 words or fewer, mostly a bare move and its name ('e4, d6', 'the knight to c3 — the Vienna'). Those short notes cluster on book moves the student's side is expected to know, or on the opponent's reply. Long notes arrive at (a) the first branch point of the opening ('the first moment with several possible variations', 3024), (b) a tempting move that fails, (c) the punish or trap moment, and (d) the moment the plan or structure is set. So the pattern is: name it and move on through known book; give the full set of points at the first decision, the trap and the plan; spend most words in the early middlegame; then go terse in conversion ('the rest is easy', 'the last step is just…'). This matches V11 (never silent; a short clause is fine) and V19 (say more where it matters). One gap: V19 asks for every opening move to be explained in full. The reference coach does not do that on routine book moves; he does it where the move is not routine. V19 already says to say less where the student's record proves they know it, so a cold-start rule of 'everything' is more than the reference coach himself says. Flag this to David as a point to settle.

rhythm: OPENING (book moves): one short clause per move that names the move and its single point ("You put the question to the bishop with a6"; "the knight to d2, not c3 — so the c-pawn can come to c3"). The opening is named the moment it appears, and alternatives are named in passing ("the Møller is …Bc5, the main move is the modest …Be7"). A run of book moves is still about one line each, never silent, and the long explanation is saved for the move where the opponent departs or the trap appears. That move gets 2-4 sentences: what the slip is, why it looks natural, the punishing move, and the line in words. EARLY MIDDLEGAME: the longest notes (3-5 sentences). The plan is stated once ("pile on d4: double rooks, knight to f5"), then each later move is one clause tied back to it. At a decision there is a short weighing of the tempting choice, why it fails and what works, plus a principle line. CRITICAL TACTICAL MOMENT: the full line in words, the forced reply named, and the condition that makes it work. CONVERSION / ENDGAME: drops to one clause or none per move: "simplify", "just push the g-pawn", "bring every piece in". The one exception is a single principle note on conversion order: king to the centre, rooks to open files, find the wing for the passed pawn. The density follows decision weight, not move number. Quiet-but-meaningful moves (a5, c6, h6, b3) always get their purpose, even mid-sequence.

summary:
Read all 1,500 notes (#4500-#5999; 100 videos; 760 opening / 592 middlegame / 148 endgame; 840 on the student's own move, 660 on the opponent's) end to end, and catalogued 97 distinct teaching acts, each mapped to verified code (file:line): 37 already computed, 48 partial, 11 missing, 1 not a computer by design.

The surprise is how much already exists. speedRunReads.ts holds about 27 of the reference coach's habits, and moveIntent, moveOrder, theirMoveCost, recaptureChoice, falseAlarm, bluffDetector, deliberation, buildRejectedTempting, tradeJudgement, conversionMethod, forkTrick, latentFork and the gem/trap-ahead computers cover most of the rest. The gap is mostly CONDITIONS and COMPARISONS, not whole computers.

OPENING GAPS (F02), highest value first:
1. The defining-move clause. openingIdentity.ts:20 computes `defining` offline, and nothing in src reads it. That is computed and then dropped (G8.5).
2. The opening's bargain in one sentence.
3. A contrast with the sibling opening.
4. On a book departure, the job the book move did that the played move doesn't.
5. Choosing, among close moves, the one that sets a trap, and setting bait.

On method: frequencies are regex counts over the slice (precision mixed, ±30%), anchored by the note ids given in each entry.
rhythm:
These figures are measured over all 1,500 notes; they are not estimates.

WORDS PER NOTE: median 23, mean 27.6, p10 6, p90 51. By phase the median is 23 in the opening, 25 in the middlegame and 18 in the endgame.
- 1-9 words: 21%
- 10-24 words: 32%
- 25-49 words: 35%
- 50-99 words: 9%
- 100+ words: 1.5%

HE SPEAKS ON ALMOST EVERY PLY (V11). Of 1,400 consecutive note pairs in the same video, 1,089 skip no ply, 194 skip one, and 117 skip two or more. Only 148 notes (10%) are bare move-narration (9 words or fewer, no reason), and two videos account for most of those.

BOTH SIDES GET EQUAL AIRTIME: median 21 words on the opponent's move vs 22 on the student's own.

THE LONG MONOLOGUES (90+ words, 25 notes) never fall in the endgame: 17 are middlegame, 7 opening, 0 endgame. They sit at decision points, often on the OPPONENT's move, where he works through the student's coming choice in advance.
- Deliberation language appears in 13% of opponent-move notes vs 10% of own-move notes.
- Notes on the student's own move open by naming the move 35% of the time, vs 24% on the opponent's move.
- So he thinks while their move is on the board, then names his move with its reason.

BY PHASE:
- Opening: 86% of opening notes (655/760) carry an explicit reason. One opening ply typically stacks the name or theory status, the idea, and what the move prepares or stops (V19 holds).
- Middlegame: the longest thoughts.
- Endgame and conversion: shorter, technique-led, often 'several moves win'.

LINKING (F0b): 48% of notes over 9 words carry an explicit link (because / so / but / instead / the point). About 7% of thoughts (104) run across two plies: a sentence starts on one move and finishes on the next.

ORDER INSIDE A LONG NOTE (matches F18; e.g. #4517, #4841, #4935-4937, #5051):
1. What their move did or threatens.
2. The candidates, with the tempting one named and refuted by a short line.
3. Not yet: first this.
4. The choice, with its one deciding reason.
5. Close on a general habit or rule.

teachingMoves.move: [OPENING] State a move's theory status: the main line, the reputable try, the move you must know, a sideline, dubious
teachingMoves.example: In the Englund, the knight to c6 is by far the most played reply and the best developing move (7130). In the King's Gambit, an early d4 has long been known as dubious because …Qh4+ forces the king to e2 (7425-7427).

teachingMoves.move: [OPENING] Give a verdict on the opponent's opening move WITH the board reason, then show how to punish it
teachingMoves.example: An early c3 against the fianchetto is called mediocre: it develops nothing, takes c3 from White's own knight and leads to passive play (6490). An early …d6 in an Open Sicilian is a slip because it lets d5 kick the knight to a bad square (6254-6255). Philidor's …d6 shuts in the bishop and develops nothing, so open the centre (7340).

teachingMoves.move: [OPENING] Move order: play this first, because the other order transposes into something worse or runs into a tactic
teachingMoves.example: In the Caro-Kann Advance, …Bf5 comes before …e6; …e6 first locks the bishop and transposes into an ordinary French (6020). In the King's Gambit, …Qh5+ waits because g4 would hit it, so …Bd6 comes first (7436).

teachingMoves.move: [OPENING] Name the rule, then the reason it bends here (rule and exception)
teachingMoves.example: Pushing the f-pawn usually weakens, but castling long makes f3 an asset that covers e4 (6786-6787). d5 would normally open their bishop's diagonal, but that bishop is about to be traded off (7203). teachingMoves.move: [OPENING] Gambit handling: what the material buys, and the strategy for each side
teachingMoves.example: A gambit buys only a development lead, so it demands speed: let them castle and you are just a pawn down (6441). rhythm: Measured over the slice (1,477 distilled notes from 85 videos; these are paraphrases, so word counts run below his raw speech, which thinkAloud.ts:1-8 measured at about 50 words a move). Median words per note: opening 19 (p90 41), middlegame 20 (p90 45), endgame 13 (p90 28). He speaks on almost every ply: in the 35 videos with 15+ notes there are about 0.79 notes per ply of the covered span. Most plies get a short clause; 8 words or fewer on 19% of opening notes, 21% of middlegame, 32% of endgame. The long notes (40 of them at 60+ words) are all opening or middlegame (19 and 21), none endgame, and every one sits at a decision: a theory fork with several named branches (6304-6309, 6604, 6617-6618, 7004), a choice between candidates (6279, 6537, 6743, 7218, 7224), a branching tactical calculation (6181, 6525-6526, 6611, 6749, 6777), or the plan after material changes (6221, 6802, 7096). Long explanations are earned by the moment, not spread evenly. About 44% of opening notes and 43% of middlegame notes are about the OPPONENT's move: he diagnoses their choice (what it wants, whether it's good, what it gave up, how to punish it) almost as often as he guides the student's. Order inside one note: (1) what the move is, or its name; (2) its job or reason; (3) what it stops, allows or gives up; (4) the tempting alternative and why it fails, or the line with their reply; (5) the habit or principle, last (e.g. 6279: the queen defends; not the bishop, which would give up the pair; if Bf4, unpin with Bd6; habit: before moving an attacked queen, look for an intermezzo). By phase: the opening carries naming, purpose, theory status, verdicts on opponent moves, traps and move order. Quiet middlegames carry plans, prophylaxis, tension and piece improvement. Critical moments carry candidates, the failing tempting move, the line, and a safety check. After winning material comes the conversion method. Endgames get terse technique labels. The weighting order when choosing a move: concrete safety (is it hanging, does it lose to a check), then the line with their replies, then structural or tempo cost, then practical factors. Flashy tries are deferred until the king is safe and the pieces are out (6517: no premature trap-setting moves unless you are losing).

MISSING, ranked by how often he does it in this slice:
1. Opening knowledge facts: a live 'main line / move to know' on the student's own move; the reason half of the opponent's opening verdict (theirOpeningVerdict at openingAnnouncement.ts:166 gives only a cost in words and is never joined with theirMoveCost.ts:60); transposition and gateway moves; closing timing windows; comparative tempo counts.
2. Pattern trigger rules ('whenever X, look for Y') with their conditions, and sacrifice patterns' when-it-fails half (F04, Q7).
3. Pin judgement rules: proximity, comparing pin strength, the kickable counter-pin, 'a pin removes a defender'.
4. Calculation and safety habits beyond methodBeat's four: start with the simplest move, look one step further, refresh after exchanges, the queen-escape check before grabbing, the in-between-check check before cashing in.
5. Golden-nugget knowledge: material imbalance rules, castling long activates the rook, bad bishops defend good pawns, doubled pawns are not as bad as feared (recaptureChoice.ts:68 always counts doubling as a drawback), the queen exploits a colour complex, self-blocking checks.
6. Attack method: fix the king, clear your own blocker (F0c OBSTACLE / REMOVE IT), choose the hunting piece.
7. Gambit-handling strategy, transfer between openings, and a choice as a statement of intent.
Practical and psychological reads (panic, bluffing, the clock) have no board fact behind them and are not computers.

HOW THE REFERENCE COACH TEACHES: one thread across moves, never isolated facts. The opponent breaks opening principles, so he keeps them. They neglect the queenside, so he attacks before he is fully developed. He pushes the h-pawn at the g3 hook. Their king walks into his bishop's pin, so g3 stops guarding h4. rhythm:
Measured on the raw transcript. The live commentary is 692 words over his 15 moves, about 46 words a move. The opening block (moves 1-5) runs about 150 words, roughly 30 a move. Routine developing or castling moves take 38-47 words. Decision moments take 2-3 times that: about 76 for d5 with the punish-the-principle-breaker method, 92 for the move-9 strategic fork (h5), and 133 for 12...Ng4+, where he calculates out loud as candidate, objection, then answer. Opponent moves get 2-5 words ('they play g3') unless something changed; then he adds a one-clause verdict ('creative, not sound', 'walked right into it'). The post-game review runs about 870 words, longer than the whole live commentary. In it he replays the opponent's errors with the better move and its reason, plays out the finish behind the resignation, refutes the alternative defences, and closes on the moral plus repertoire advice. The intro is about 210 words.

The order inside one move (moves 7, 9, 12 and 14), with his self-questions recurring at step 3:
1. Name their move, with a short verdict if any.
2. Say what it changed or neglected.
3. Ask himself a question: what's left to do, do I want to rush this, what am I thinking about.
4. Weigh: on one hand / on the other, or candidate, objection, answer.
5. Play the move with its purpose ('to pry open the h-file').
6. Say what it now threatens and the opponent's one reply.
7. Sometimes add a foreshadow ('keep an eye on g3') or the method line ('don't panic, finish developing, attack when ready').

The speed-run study of two other games measured about 25-30 words a move: lead with the question or the threat, then the reason, then a 2-4-ply proof. He talks about what the opponent WANTS more than what a piece eyes. The census adds that he explains EVERY move, book moves included; nothing goes quiet for being routine.

By phase:
- Opening: principle plus purpose on every move, and the opening's identity and purpose at the start.
- Middlegame: plans, weighing and calculated lines, at 2-3 times the words.
- Endgame: not reached in this game. Census: endgame technique is about 1.2% of his lines, push-or-hold about 0.4%; conversion advice appears whenever he is winning.
- Low-rated opponents (700): safety, principle and the principle's exception, asked as questions.
- High-rated opponents (2300): plan and method.

summary:
TEACHING TRACK: how the reference coach teaches, each act mapped to the code. Read end to end: RULEBOOK.md, questions.md, the duplicate census, 2026-09-29 full review + all of danya-review-2026-09-29/ (parts 0-7, sources, both tapes, the five brainstorm-r1 reports), the 2026-09-16 behaviour audit, every file in data/sources/danielnaroditsky-voice/, plus the 09-17 structures study, 09-24 speedrun target, 09-27 census, 08-23 coverage matrix, docs/naroditsky-insight-catalogue.md, the swarm-input transcript, and the two tape games in public/data/voiced-teachings.json. Every computer named was opened, not recalled.

HOW HE TEACHES, IN ONE PARAGRAPH. A game is one story. He names the opening and says where it stands. He turns the opponent's first concession into the game's single thesis (a target square, a weak pawn, a break) and points later beats back at it. On every move he asks what the opponent's move changed or gave up. He states a principle and then its exception, because the circumstances changed. At the few moments that matter he thinks out loud: the candidates, each rejected with a short line played to where it lands, then the move with its reason. His habits are concrete triggers: count before you take, list the loose pieces, the three answers to a check, take the escape square first, check for an in-between move before recapturing. He converts by a named method chosen by the size of the edge. Afterwards he rewinds to the 2-5 decision points ("if they X, you Y"), prunes the side branches and closes on takeaways. He rarely waits for an answer; his questions are rhetorical and answered in the same breath. He names the move with its reason (supports S3/F05).

CATALOGUE COUNT (73 acts). About 44 built, 16 partial, 13 missing. The breadth is mostly built: the WO-TEACH-GAPS beats, the census computers (moveIntent, moveOrder, theirMoveCost, kingAttack, recaptureChoice, ruleException, falseAlarm, pushOrHold), about 26 reads in speedRunReads.ts, about 20 in moveInsight.ts, and the endgame and concept engines.

What is missing is the chain and the selection, not the facts:
1. No decider has a thesis or relevance term. grep for 'thesis' in coachDecider.ts, factSelector.ts, learnTurnDoor.ts and voicePackage.ts finds nothing. teachingSelector.ts:192/:347 builds a thesis only for Review, phase narration and openings.
2. The think-aloud producer (thinkAloud.ts:226 depthClauses) has one caller, positionFacts.ts:1009. It ranks clauses with a fixed table (positionFacts.ts:1009-1018: not-yet 90, stop-flaw 70, line 60, hole-access 50, speedrun-read 45), not by computed stakes.
3. Its documented step 'what I still owe' (thinkAloud.ts:5) has no clause kind (thinkAloud.ts:192).
4. Review (coachFeatureService.ts:2308) and Tactics (puzzleMethod.ts:41) call decide() directly and never get the think-aloud depth (F18 note confirmed).

MISSING COMPUTERS (bring to David; new per B6):
- A pin that breaks with tempo: pinGeometry.ts:135 isRealPin has no test for check, a bigger threat or a discovery.
- 'A pinned defender is not a defender': computed silently at whyItFailed.ts:134/:374, never spoken.
- A trap pattern taught with its conditions, and the unsound-sacrifice explanation (S12): moveInsight.ts:668 greekGift speaks only when the engine's best move is the sacrifice.
- The king that walks a diagonal and chases two goals at once.
- Honest 'this is murky'.
- Structure transfer by colour flip ('the reversed X, a tempo up'): only 3 hand-mapped structures at positionReadingService.ts:1041-1052.
- The 'if they X, you Y; if Z, then W' fork statement: deleted (opponentIntent.ts:88-96, comment at :93-95); the data still sits in OpponentPlan (:68-85).
- The opponent's concession turned into a named recipe.
- Per-student term memory (V18): learnMemory.ts:277 clears it every game.
- Repeats that shrink across games: the standingRefrains.ts:227 ledger is per game.
- Tree triage in the rewind.
- An opponent clock and speed read.
- A label lexicon.
- A least-valuable-piece advisor.
- Value of a defensive piece.
- 'What they wrongly believe'.
- Practical vs objective outside the pro-rep seam (courseWhyFacts.ts:84).
- Praise for a dodged habit (V6).

DUPLICATES FOUND WHILE MAPPING (F2/R5):
- The recapture reflex has 3 computers: kneeJerk.ts:15 (Learn, learnBoardTeaching.ts:180), moveInsight.ts:642 autopilotRecapture (Puzzles, PuzzleBoard.tsx:652) and safetyHabits.ts:42. The first two answer the same question with different gates.
- 'What their move gave up' has 4: moveInsight.ts:573/:523, theirMoveCost.ts:60, backwardLook.ts:470, concessionBeat.ts:131.
- 'What a move is for' has 2: moveIntent.ts:124 and deliberation.ts:354.
- Piece routes have 2: forwardTeaching.ts:186 and positionReadingService.ts:893.
- Trade verdicts have 2: tradeJudgement.ts:40 and tradeQuality.ts:124.
- The 'behind? complicate' line is written 5 times: reviewConcepts.ts:123, positionCharacter.ts:103, groundedAnswer.ts:1338, principleVoice.ts:437, moveInsight.ts:990.

A CAP THAT CONTRADICTS HIM. He plays a line to where it lands. sayLine is capped at 4 plies (thinkAloud.ts:114 maxPlies = 4), and the line's outcome is judged on 4 plies (thinkAloud.ts:280). This conflicts with S10 and G4.5.

SURFACE GAPS:
- The corpus-rate behaviour registry runs on Learn only: src/services/danyaBehaviors.ts:888, called once at CoachTeachPage.tsx:8726.
- mastersPlanRead is a Learn-only lane (computerRoles.ts:46).
- A real-game citation reaches Review (reviewStoryGame.ts:134) and opening identity (openingIdentity.ts:144). Learn and the lessons never reach for one.

DATA CONFIRMS F02. 48% of his beats are in the opening, and the densest, longest stretch is moves 7-12, where the thesis and the break are declared.

CAVEAT. The voiced corpus is our LLM rewrite of his structure, so the rhythm numbers measure his structure, not his words.
rhythm:
Measured on public/data/voiced-teachings.json (7,477 beats; 360 games with at least 5 in-game beats, cut at the first ply reset where the rewind starts).

LENGTH. A spoken beat is short: median 20 words (p25 10, p75 31, p90 46, p99 110).

DENSITY. 65% of in-game plies carry a beat. The per-game median is 74% (IQR 42-88%). The rest are bare or silent routine plies: book moves, recaptures, the opponent's filler.

BY PHASE.
- Opening: 3,617 beats (48% of all), median 20 words.
- Middlegame: 2,901 beats (39%), median 21 words, p90 50. The longest.
- Endgame: 959 beats (13%), median 15 words. Technique is said tersely.

BY PLY BAND.
- Moves 1-6: 61% of plies spoken, median 18 words. He names the opening, places it, and gives the principle of each move.
- Moves 7-12: 71% spoken, median 23 words. The densest and longest stretch: the opponent's concession is named, the thesis is declared, the break is chosen.
- Plies 25-50: 66% spoken, median 19 words.
- Plies 51 and later: 58% spoken, median 14 words. Conversion is clipped to the method plus the tactic.

LIVE COMMENTARY IS ABOUT 2.5 TIMES LONGER than the distilled beats. thinkAloud.ts:2-3 measured the swarm-input transcript at about 50 words a move: 20-47 on a routine move, 90-133 at a decision.

THE SHAPE IS BIMODAL. Most beats carry ONE idea plus its reason. Monologues of 5-15 ideas cluster only at the critical moment and in the post-game rewind. In 60-70% of videos the rewind is a second pass longer than the game itself.

TAPE COMPARISON (game 3UqPa5eV2e0, 1870).
- He spoke 20 beats over 42 plies. He was silent through the whole opening shuffle (plies 8-13), and his two longest beats were the thesis (ply 14) and the break (ply 15).
- Our Learn spoke 1.29 sentences per ply against his 0.60, never skipped a move pair, and stacked 3-4 unrelated facts on quiet moves.

RECONCILIATION WITH V11 (never silent). A routine ply gets one short clause (who moved, what it is for). The decider varies the LENGTH and the number of ideas, never whether a move gets a word.

rhythm:
He comments on every move.
- 31 of the 187 notes cover two or more plies as one unit, usually a capture with its recapture or a move with the obvious reply.
- In one fast game, 13 quiet plies become a single sentence (n102).

Length per note (distilled corpus):
- Overall: mean 26 words, median 21.
- Opening: 87 notes, median 23.
- Middlegame: 86 notes, median 21.
- Endgame: 14 notes, median 13.5.

Bare narration of 8 words or fewer:
- Opening 4 of 87, middlegame 9 of 86, endgame 5 of 14.
- Speech shrinks as the result becomes a matter of technique.

Long notes happen only at a decision with a tempting wrong option. Eight notes run over 60 words:
- n66 (190 words): the whole middlegame plan, given at the knight-development decision.
- n91 (131), n88 (126), n92 (122) and n100 (100): the f4-break deliberation.
- n132 (74), n72 (65) and n124 (64).

Their moves get as much breath as the student's: 85 notes averaging 25 words, against 102 averaging 27. Explanatory games run 30 to 42 words a note. Fast attacking or converting games run 17 to 18.

Order inside a decision note:
1. What their move did, cost or wants.
2. Flag the moment.
3. The natural or tempting candidates.
4. Each candidate's flaw, as a short line with their reply or as the squares it gives up.
5. The move.
6. The move's jobs.
7. The next step of the plan.
8. A callback or a teaser.

Order on their move: what it hits, then a verdict (sound, passive or rare), then what they want, then what it cost them, then the student's answer.

Several linked thoughts on one move is normal at decisions, and only there.

Contrast with the code:
- Learn's turn door holds back an unstaked "aside" that shares no square with the lead (learnTurnDoor.ts:413-416). Most of the plan content in these notes carries no material stake, so it would be held back.
- The door's own comment puts his rate at 35 to 50 words a move, against 80 to 95 for an unheld Learn turn (learnTurnDoor.ts:406-411).
- thinkAloud.ts:3-4 measured about 50 words a move on the raw transcript of the first game in this slice, roughly twice the distilled notes.

teachingMoves.example: That h-pawn push only loosens their own king (n15). Offering to trade their fianchetto bishop shows the setup's weakness, because the holes it covered stay (n36). Their bishop now just props up a pawn (n40). Their quiet d6 shuts in the bishop on e7 (n130). A pawn on d3 instead of d4 hands you d4 (n176).
teachingMoves.when: Their pawn moves and passive developing moves
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. theirMoveCost.ts:60 covers hole (:72-91), bishop-shut (:94-115), castling and structure. It deliberately strips 'pawn cover thinned' (theirMoveCost.ts:144), and kingAttack.ts:71 fires only on the attacker's own move, so their self-weakening h-pawn push (n15) has no Learn lane. describeNotableMove (reviewTeachingPoints.ts:557) is Review-only, called at coachFeatureService.ts:3206. MISSING: 'their piece is now tied to defending a pawn' (n40) and 'they are offering to trade the piece that guards their weak colour' (n36).

teachingMoves.move: Their maneuver, where it is heading, and the real point of an earlier move
teachingMoves.example: Their knight goes from c6 to e7 and on to g6 (n73). The knight jumps to h5, aiming for f4 (n87). They take on c5, which was the point of their bishop move, and now they are tied to that pawn (n44).
teachingMoves.when: An opponent maneuver in progress, or the move that cashes in an earlier one
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. moveIntent.ts:124, run from their seat (theirIntent lane, computerRoles.ts:84), states the purpose at the time of the move. stepArc (planArc.ts:236) tracks aims across moves. MISSING: the look-back 'that was the point of their earlier move', said on the move that pays it off.

teachingMoves.move: Ask why they did it, then refute their plan with the line
teachingMoves.example: Why did their knight go to the edge? They want ...f5. But once the pawns and pieces trade on f5, your g-pawn forks their rook and knight at the end (n88).
teachingMoves.when: An odd-looking opponent move
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. buildOpponentIntent (opponentIntent.ts:55) gives their top ideas plus your reply, taken from ply 2 of each line. proofForMover (exchangeLedger.ts:481) counts the trades. latentFork.ts:161 handles knights only (latentFork.ts:27), so a PAWN fork at the end of an exchange sequence is not found. MISSING: composing their idea, then the exchange line, then the fork that ends it.

teachingMoves.move: Verdict on how dangerous their idea is (harmless, unsound or toothless) and why
teachingMoves.example: Not a dangerous line, so nothing special is needed: just develop (n34). Inventive, but it doesn't hold up (n17). You could stop the pin with h3, but it bites on nothing here because their pieces are too passive (n76). Their h-pawn lunge threatens nothing: meet h4 with g4, and a sacrifice would fail with too few attackers against your king (n140). The check is harmless because g1 is free (n154).
teachingMoves.when: An aggressive-looking but empty opponent move, or a pin or sacrifice the student could head off
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. bluffDetector.ts:37 handles PIECES only (knight, bishop, rook, queen; bluffDetector.ts:43), so pawn lunges are left out. falseAlarm.ts:37 needs a real threat. countKingAttack (kingSafety.ts:297) has the attacker and defender counts. MISSING: 'this pin is toothless, nothing can pile on it' (pinPressure.ts:1-18 computes only the positive case), and a pawn-storm bluff judged by attacker count.

teachingMoves.move: Credit their correct defence or good move
teachingMoves.example: They find the right reply (n63). The knight on g6 is the correct setup here (n79). They are handling this very well (n93). They sidestep the little trick (n102). A good move (n103). A solid way past the traps (n118).
teachingMoves.when: The opponent avoids the student's trap or finds the best or only move
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. threatStoppedBy (opponentMovePurpose.ts:58) feeds the theirPurpose lane (computerRoles.ts:83) and says which of the student's threats their move stopped. Review has fixed stems only for a 'brilliant' opponent move (coachFeatureService.ts:1175-1177). MISSING: 'they sidestepped the trap here' for mined gems; forkTrick.ts:126 covers only the fork-trick family.

teachingMoves.move: Counterfactual for their alternative: had they played X, you'd answer Y
teachingMoves.example: Had they pinned on g4 instead, you would chase the bishop with h3 and could follow with g4 (n77). Their ...b5 was no danger anyway, because e5 answers it (n143).
teachingMoves.when: Right after the opponent chose between natural moves
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. opponentIntent.ts:55 gives the branched preview BEFORE their move. Nothing speaks the branch after it.

teachingMoves.move: Their only defence: name it, and say whether they found it
teachingMoves.example: Their king walks straight into a knight check (n19). Their only real move was the retreat; instead they let you take with check (n22). Only the rook to e1 stops the mate (n29). They have a single move to save the knight (n56).
teachingMoves.when: After the student's threat, or when they miss their one defence
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. criticalMoment.ts:6-11 counts the moves that hold, but Learn uses it for the STUDENT's decision (criticalMoment.ts:287). opponentGap.ts:38 flags the gift without naming the one defence they missed. MISSING: 'only one move holds for THEM' after the student's threat.

teachingMoves.move: Name their standing resource or most testing setup, to keep in mind
teachingMoves.example: In this structure they always have the b4 break, so remember it (n46). Their most testing plan is the fianchetto setup (n175).
teachingMoves.when: Once the structure fixes the opponent's options
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. findPawnBreaks (positionReadingService.ts:400) works only for the side to move; opponentIntent.ts:55 gives their next moves. MISSING: the opponent's standing strategic resource in a structure.

teachingMoves.move: Name their looming tactic in advance, calmly
teachingMoves.example: They are eyeing the classic bishop sacrifice on h7. It is unpleasant, but not the end (n108-109). Their queen to f3 is the frightening idea, and here is why you hold (n100).
teachingMoves.when: The opponent has a sacrifice or strike available
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. greekGift (moveInsight.ts:668) recognizes the bishop sacrifice for the side to move, which in practice is the student's seat, through positionAsk and positionPosed. detectNewThreat (groundedAnswer.ts:6890) counts mate-in-1, forks and SEE gains, not a speculative sacrifice. MISSING for the opponent's seat.

teachingMoves.move: Flag the decision moment before explaining it
teachingMoves.example: This is the moment to learn from (n13). This is the key decision, the one most people miss (n66). It is harder than it seems (n124). Careful here (n139).
teachingMoves.when: A strategic fork in the road, even when the engine gap is small
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. criticalMomentStatement (criticalMoment.ts:287) fires only on the count of engine moves that hold (criticalMoment.ts:6-11). anyMoveFine (speedRunReads.ts:68) says the opposite, 'no move here is a big decision', whenever the top three moves sit inside the inaccuracy bar after move 8 (speedRunReads.ts:70-74). That is the shape of many strategic forks. MISSING: a flag for strategic decisions.

teachingMoves.move: List the candidates, then the one board feature that decides between them
teachingMoves.example: You could keep developing or castle long, but their whole queenside is still asleep, so start the attack now with h5 (n13-14). e5 is possible, but e6 keeps the centre closed on purpose (n43). Bg5 catches the eye, but h6 just sends it back, so play Be3 (n84). f4 is premature, Be3 runs into Ng4 and Bg5 allows the fork trick, so play Bb3 (n124).
teachingMoves.when: Every real choice in the opening and early middlegame
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. deliberationFacts (deliberation.ts:246) weighs only alternatives proved by a line, a dropped piece or a queen trade (reasonedAlternatives at deliberation.ts:278), and stays silent otherwise (:260). MISSING: positional reasons for ruling a candidate out (squares abandoned, the structure it leads to, a tempo lost to a kick). Also missing: development counted BY WING. homeMinorCount (development.ts:63) is a total, and at n13 both sides had exactly one minor at home.

teachingMoves.move: Hold back the tempting move, then explain it by the squares it gives up
teachingMoves.example: e5 is tempting, but wait. On the next move: it would leave f5 and e6 weak and take support away from d5, so check which squares a pawn stops guarding before you push it (n48-49).
teachingMoves.when: A tempting pawn push the student should skip
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. findConcession (concessionBeat.ts:131) computes 'pawn-weakened' and 'outpost-conceded', but is called only for moves already PLAYED (backwardLook.ts:180, :305). The no-longer-guarded squares in describeNotableMove (reviewTeachingPoints.ts:596-616) cover wing pawns only and run in Review only. MISSING for an unplayed candidate.

teachingMoves.move: Keep the tension when the recapture would help their worst piece
teachingMoves.example: Taking on d4 would only centralize their bishop. Leave it, develop, and let them be the one to release the tension (n41). Put your own pawn in contact and make their pawn decide (n39).
teachingMoves.when: Central pawn contact with a capture available
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. keepTension (speedRunReads.ts:49) says releasing the tension 'helps them', but not HOW (which of their pieces the recapture improves). The reason is MISSING.

teachingMoves.move: Choose the structure on purpose
teachingMoves.example: Being able to open the centre is not a reason to do it. Keep it closed and outplay them there (n43). Skip the reflex e5: against this setup c5 heads for a Dragon-type structure and claims d4 (n176-177).
teachingMoves.when: Two pawn moves of similar value that lead to different structures
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING. namedPawnStructure (positionReadingService.ts:1060) names only the CURRENT structure. flexibleFirst (speedRunReads.ts:549) compares a piece move against a pawn move by flexibility only.

teachingMoves.move: When a piece is chased: keep it working, keep it central, keep it linked
teachingMoves.example: Keep the bishop on its strong diagonal instead of letting them push it somewhere worse (n50). Bring the knight back toward the centre, not the edge. Knights that guard each other are healthy, and this one can go to c4 later (n51).
teachingMoves.when: A piece is kicked
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. Existing: 'keep-working' (moveFundamentals.ts:56) and computePieceRoute (forwardTeaching.ts:186) for the later route. MISSING: linked knights, i.e. two knights protecting each other, as a fact.

teachingMoves.move: Not yet, first this, and the square that makes it work
teachingMoves.example: Don't grab on h4 yet. First get your bishop out of trouble with tempo, then take (n23). You don't have to take the knight: capture on c5 first, and now their queen check is not mate because your g3 pawn covers h4 (n95-96).
teachingMoves.when: A capture is available but a forcing or safety move should come first
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: COVERED by notYet (thinkAloud.ts:145, written from n23's game), secureFirst (speedRunReads.ts:178) and moveOrder.ts:65. These speak only where the move may be named (gate at thinkAloud.ts:262). The square-coverage reason ('g3 covers h4, so it isn't mate') is PARTIAL: moveOrder explains an order by material only (ORDER_COST_CP at moveOrder.ts:29), and escapeSquareFirst (moveInsight.ts:701) is its mirror.

teachingMoves.move: Prefer the simpler win
teachingMoves.example: You could bring the queen over, but simpler is to take the bishop (n148). Just take back and stay two pieces up (n158). Simpler than grabbing b7 is doubling on f7 (n164).
teachingMoves.when: Winning, with several good moves
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING. readConversion (conversionMethod.ts:44) gives a plan step, not a choice between two winning moves by risk.

teachingMoves.move: Don't invite even a harmless risk, and don't repair their structure
teachingMoves.example: That check would be harmless, but why allow it? Put the queen on f5 and force the trade (n151). Taking on e6 yourself would only fix their pawns (n152).
teachingMoves.when: Winning positions with several safe paths
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING. recaptureChoice.ts:103 compares the student's own recaptures, and tradeJudgement.ts:40 needs a capture by the student followed by their recapture. Nothing judges a capture by what it does to THEIR structure.

teachingMoves.move: Take a practical risk to play for a win
teachingMoves.example: Taking on f3 is risky, but in this equal position it is the only way to play for a win (n104-105).
teachingMoves.when: Equal positions where the student needs to win
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING. This is the census's 'practical play', and no board computer covers it.

teachingMoves.move: One move, several jobs
teachingMoves.example: The knight jump hits the bishop, threatens to wreck their pawns, and if the bishop steps away you take on c5 and win your pawn back (n45). The knight back to g1 guards h3 and frees the f-pawn (n90). The queen on d3 covers c4 and stops b5 (n143). The queen heads for h5, gathering pieces, hitting the knight and building mating chances (n55).
teachingMoves.when: Almost every student move
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: COVERED or PARTIAL. moveIntent.ts:124 (prevents plus prepares gives two jobs), extraJobs (deliberation.ts:354; guard plus x-ray) and the MoveFundamentalId list (moveFundamentals.ts:34-71). The conditional second point ('if they do X, then Y') is not composed.

teachingMoves.move: The line in words, with their reply, ending on what it achieves and tied back to the plan
teachingMoves.example: You are looking at a knight check on g4. They can take it, but you recapture with the pawn and the h-file opens, which was the goal all along (n19-20). The knight takes, you take back, the queen checks, and your king simply steps to g2 (n92). After the queens come off on f5, the pin wins more material (n153).
teachingMoves.when: Whenever a forcing idea is the reason for a move
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: COVERED by sayLine (thinkAloud.ts:114) and lineAchieves (thinkAloud.ts:71), which cover file, king cover and promotion, with material and mate handled by proofForMover (exchangeLedger.ts:481); the lines are arrowed. The callback to a plan announced EARLIER is PARTIAL: payoffFor (learnBoardTeaching.ts:917) fires only when the STUDENT's own move lands on the promised square.

teachingMoves.move: The objection IS the point: a decoy or sacrifice that opens lines
teachingMoves.example: Yes, they can take the knight, and that is exactly the idea (n20). The queen swings across and gives up the rook (n26-27).
teachingMoves.when: Sacrifices and decoys
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. playAnyway (speedRunReads.ts:267) handles a scary reply on the engine line that still holds. lineAchieves (thinkAloud.ts:71) covers 'the file opens toward their king'. describeSacBreaksKingShield (reviewSacrifice.ts:149) is Review-only and needs a capture next to the king.

teachingMoves.move: King attack: open lines and let the pieces pour in
teachingMoves.example: Once that pawn goes, all your pieces join the attack (n30). The queen to h5 lines up on their king (n55).
teachingMoves.when: Attacking a castled king
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: COVERED by kingAttack.ts:71 (kinds listed at kingAttack.ts:26), which counts with countKingAttack (kingSafety.ts:297).

teachingMoves.move: Compensation: what the material or the concession buys
teachingMoves.example: You are a rook short, yet their king cannot hold off the attack (n28). The trade doubles your pawns, but you get the two bishops and c4 to support the centre (n75, 78).
teachingMoves.when: Sacrifices, or accepting a structural concession
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. sacrificeCompensation (reviewSacrifice.ts:44) is Review-only (reviewFullData.ts:915, coachFeatureService.ts:2750) and reads only king-in-centre and development lead. recaptureChoice.ts:103 speaks only the DIFFERENCE between two recaptures and returns null when there is just one (recaptureChoice.ts:115). So n78's trade-off, doubled pawns for the bishop pair, is MISSING.

teachingMoves.move: A chain of consequences from a natural plan move
teachingMoves.example: Put the knight on d2 and their queen comes to d7, forcing g4, and g4 kills the f4 square you are preparing to break on (n89). After f4, exf4, gxf4 and ...f5, the centre opens, their queen eyes your e3 bishop, and taking on f4 drops e4 (n91).
teachingMoves.when: Before committing to a plan move
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING. causalChain.ts:1-12 and :639 walk BACKWARD from a material tactic. Nothing chains forward through the engine's reply to a consequence for the plan, such as killing your own break.

teachingMoves.move: Weigh the remedies for a flawed plan
teachingMoves.example: Adding another defender to f4 doesn't fix it. Shielding the bishop would, but there is no time (n91).
teachingMoves.when: A planned break that fails right now
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING.

teachingMoves.move: Switch plans, and name the conflict between two plans
teachingMoves.example: Shelve f4 and open a second front with h4; the g3 pawn backs it up. And once your pawn reaches h5, f4 would only expose your own king (n92-93).
teachingMoves.when: The first plan proves flawed
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. stepArc (planArc.ts:236) tracks plans that emerge, advance, arrive or drop. But AimKind has no pawn-BREAK aim (planArc.ts:31), so it cannot see a shelved break plan.

teachingMoves.move: Does their sacrifice work? Check it and say the result
teachingMoves.example: Does the knight jump work? The lines go deep: it holds to a perpetual, nothing more (n95). Now the capture works, but only with exact moves (n98).
teachingMoves.when: An opponent sacrifice or a forced sequence
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL and ORPHANED. walkForcedSequence (onlyMoveSequence.ts:57) proves 'every move is the only move, and it ends in a perpetual', but nothing in src imports it outside its own file.

teachingMoves.move: It only LOOKS like a trap
teachingMoves.example: Bishop to h3 seems to trap your queen, but your knight takes the bishop and defends the queen in one move. The same knight also blocks their perpetual on h3 (n100).
teachingMoves.when: An opponent's scary tactical try
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING. trappedOnBoard (reviewTeachingPoints.ts:804) asserts that a piece is trapped, and its rescue scan only keeps it silent. Nothing explains why an apparent trap fails.

teachingMoves.move: Two ways to win: name both
teachingMoves.example: If they play e3, take the rook back; or play Bg4, with mating ideas everywhere (n31-32).
teachingMoves.when: Winning positions
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. readConversion (conversionMethod.ts:44) gives one step, and deliberation lists alternatives only by their shortfall.

teachingMoves.move: An x-ray through their attacked piece decides where it can go
teachingMoves.example: Hit the knight with the queen. Their bishop sits behind it on the same diagonal, so the knight can only go where it still protects the bishop (n4-5).
teachingMoves.when: Attacking a piece that shields another piece on a line
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING. pinGeometry.ts:146 rejects a pin unless the rear piece is worth MORE, so an equal bishop behind a knight fails. findXrays requires a FRIENDLY blocker (positionReadingService.ts:860).

teachingMoves.move: A discovered attack through your own piece gains time on a loose piece
teachingMoves.example: Your queen looks through your own f3 knight at their unprotected knight on h5. Move your knight, which you wanted to do anyway, and theirs has to retreat (n88).
teachingMoves.when: An undefended enemy piece behind one of your own pieces on a line
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING. findXrays keeps only targets worth MORE than the attacking piece (positionReadingService.ts:851), so a queen x-raying a loose minor piece is dropped.

teachingMoves.move: Watch your own lines and soft spots, and confirm nothing reaches them yet
teachingMoves.example: With your king on h2, keep an eye on a sudden knight check (n150). Keep an eye on the long diagonal to your king, though no check reaches it now (n158). Don't forget the h3 pawn (n137). Once the centre opens, their queen eyes your e3 bishop (n91).
teachingMoves.when: After the king moves, or when a line may open
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. detectLatentDanger (latentDanger.ts:87) needs two of your pieces lined up with at most one piece shielding them. detectKingExposure (kingSafety.ts:56) flags a broken pawn shelter with an enemy piece aimed at it, but never says 'watch this line, nothing reaches it yet'. looseOwnPieces (moveInsight.ts:947) and heldByTactic (speedRunReads.ts:167) skip pawns, so a pawn about to be hit by a battery (n137) goes unsaid.

teachingMoves.move: Before you jump, check who guards the landing square
teachingMoves.example: The knight wants c4 to hit their queen, but their knight on a3 already covers c4 (n56).
teachingMoves.when: Planning a knight jump
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. landingIsSafe (positionReadingService.ts:155) has the fact, but no lane teaches it as a habit (methodBeat.ts:291).

teachingMoves.move: Restrict their piece, then trap it
teachingMoves.example: Their e6 bishop has nowhere left to go, so f4 comes naturally. Keep it from escaping and f5 wins it. That also tells you where your queen belongs: d3, covering c4 (n141-145). Your pawn push should drive the knight into the corner (n94).
teachingMoves.when: An enemy minor piece with few squares
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING for the attacking side. noRetreat (moveInsight.ts:957) can read either side but is called only with the student's own pieces (moveInsight.ts:287, :751). trappedOnBoard handles rooks and queens only, and only once they are attacked (reviewTeachingPoints.ts:812). awkwardBlock (speedRunReads.ts:244) covers blocks forced by a check only.

teachingMoves.move: The hook: a pawn lever against their castled king
teachingMoves.example: Development isn't finished, but the attack can start: h5, to open the h-file at their g3 pawn (n14).
teachingMoves.when: The opponent has castled behind a pawn that your pawn can reach
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: COVERED as a computation: pawnHook (moveInsight.ts:782) finds this exact shape. In Learn it reaches the student only through positionAsk on the Hint button and in drills (CoachTeachPage.tsx:11968, :11939, :2870), not at the moment the plan is chosen.

teachingMoves.move: Mark the sacrificial target in advance
teachingMoves.example: That g3 pawn is where a sacrifice may land (n16).
teachingMoves.when: Your pieces are converging on one pawn in front of their king
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING. latentDanger.ts:87 reads only the student's own camp, and kingAttack.ts:71 fires on a move rather than forecasting the target.

teachingMoves.move: Fix their wing pawn with yours, or provoke it and then freeze it
teachingMoves.example: Don't push your h-pawn first. Let them push, then freeze their pawn with h3; a pawn that comes forward becomes a target (n66). Answer h4 with h5, not the popular h6: it clamps g4 and the break is gone (n182-183).
teachingMoves.when: A flank pawn advance by either side
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. provokes (speedRunReads.ts:125) says a provoked pawn becomes a target, read from the engine line. MISSING: blocking a wing pawn thrust with your own pawn.

teachingMoves.move: A piece can veto their break, and the bonus is revealed later
teachingMoves.example: The knight on d4 had a second, quieter job: it took away the g4 break. If they push g4 anyway, you take the bishop and recapture with your structure intact (n185).
teachingMoves.when: After an outpost move, once their break is gone
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. moveIntent.ts:124 (PREVENTS, engine-proven) can say this at the time of the move. The delayed 'hidden bonus' is MISSING (see the teaser act).

teachingMoves.move: The key-square battle: occupy it and clamp it
teachingMoves.example: c5, then Nc6, and d4 is yours without a fight. The knight settles there and goes after the bishop pair (n177-179, 184).
teachingMoves.when: A hole in their structure
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. Existing: the 'hole' case in theirMoveCost.ts:72-91; isOutpost (outpost.ts:39); the outpost plan in nextPlans.ts:161; rightPieceForHole (speedRunReads.ts:337). MISSING: counting who controls the key square.

teachingMoves.move: Golden nugget: a weakness is worth the defenders it ties down
teachingMoves.example: Put your rook on the half-open c-file against the c3 pawn. If they guard it with a rook, that rook is stuck there. That matters more than the pawn itself, because you can switch wings and they can't (n54).
teachingMoves.when: A weak pawn on a half-open file
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. moveInsight.ts:298-302 names 'a target on a file your rooks can use' (Hint and drill paths only). The 'tie their whole army to babysitting it' line exists only for ISOLATED pawns (nextPlans.ts:262, plan 3 at :231). heavyTiedDown (moveInsight.ts:1022) is called only for the student's own pieces (moveInsight.ts:288).

teachingMoves.move: Golden nugget: trade off their fianchetto bishop and its colour stays weak
teachingMoves.example: Take the bishop. It guarded the light squares around their king, and those holes never heal (n36-37).
teachingMoves.when: A trade offer involving a fianchettoed bishop
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. findColorComplexWeakness (positionReadingService.ts:676) gives a static read: at least 2 holes in that side's half and an enemy piece that can use them. TradeReason (tradeJudgement.ts:24) has no colour-complex reason, so the trade itself is never judged this way.

teachingMoves.move: Golden nugget: note every loose enemy piece the moment it appears
teachingMoves.example: That knight on h3 has no guard, so remember it: anything that hits it later is a real resource (n38). Twenty plies later the queen goes after it (n55-56).
teachingMoves.when: The opponent leaves a piece undefended with no tactic yet
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. findLoosePieces (loosePieces.ts:35) has the fact. looseTrigger.ts:14 speaks only when the engine's best QUIET move hits the piece now. The 'note it now, it pays later' promise is MISSING, and the existing promise memory expires after 16 plies (learnBoardTeaching.ts:897), which is shorter than this payoff.

teachingMoves.move: Golden nugget: in a locked centre, the setup matters more than the move order
teachingMoves.example: Once the centre is blocked, the exact order of moves stops mattering much. Aim for the right setup and plan (n79-80).
teachingMoves.when: The centre locks
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING as teaching. The fact is computed and then dropped: structureSignature.lockedCenter (boardStructure.ts:303, :341) has no reader. The only consumer of structureSignature (groundedAnswer.ts:2250) reads queensideMajority.

teachingMoves.move: Golden nugget: don't put a piece in front of the pawn you need for the break
teachingMoves.example: Not the natural Nf3 but Ne2, so the f-pawn stays free for f4-f5 (n66). The knight goes back to g1 and the f-pawn is free again (n90).
teachingMoves.when: Developing in a pawn-chain structure
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING. retreatKeepsBreak (speedRunReads.ts:421) covers the reverse case, and even it misses n90. summary:
Close second reading of voiced-teachings.json notes[187..373]: 187 notes from 8 videos (KID fianchetto game, Najdorf lecture, Italian Bb4+/Nxe4 line, Rossolimo with dxc6, Scotch, a deliberate knight-sacrifice defence lesson, an early-Qh5 game, plus the tail of an English game). The insight catalogue had already mined part of this slice (it read 0ipLPOAN_m8 as game 8; its A1 and A12 entries come from 1PI3 and 1671), and four built computers cite these notes in their headers: moveTiming.ts:1 (#310), moveContrast.ts:1 (#312), recaptureChoice.ts:2 (the dxc6 idea), and the census build status (the Kh1-prepares-f4 move from 1PI3). I catalogued 77 distinct acts. About 18 have no computer and no entry in the catalogue, census or speedrun-target doc (grep-checked).

NEW acts with no computer:
- a counterfactual pattern: 'if their queen stood here, the knight jump would fork' (#284)
- their good move's future drawback: the knight is left with no home after their own e4 (#203)
- their piece placement hands you a tempo later: the queen on f6 invites a knight to d5 (#342)
- a threat met by making it cost them: h3, so if they play the skewer anyway you take the other bishop (#363). threatAnswer.ts:7-13 has no such class.
- the quiet strengthening move is the real danger (#371)
- their move made your break possible (#289). theirMoveChanged (moveInsight.ts:573) and readTiming (moveTiming.ts:47) miss this.
- material arithmetic toward level: a piece is worth three pawns (#349-350)
- a trade that thins their attack helps the defender (#361)
- a numbered argument carried across plies (#264-266)
- temporary vs permanent drawback (#302)
- a two-sided ledger between pieces (#309)
- a modest square justified by its duties (#290-291)
- the best defence both improves and sets a trap (#343)
- a pin that only looks like a pin. pinGeometry.ts:135 decides it, but nothing says it (#196).
- surprise value of a sound but rarely known move (#278)
- an indirectly defended pawn (#216). takeTheSting (speedRunReads.ts:400) and heldByTactic (:162) both skip pawns.
- the drawback → condition → remedy composite (#295). The pieces exist; no composer joins them.

Conflicts and decisions for David (B6):
1. #361 conflicts with code. 'Behind → keep pieces on, every trade helps them' is stated unconditionally in 5 places: moveInsight.ts:1012, tradeJudgement.ts:78, positionCharacter.ts:103, principleVoice.ts:437, reviewConcepts.ts:123. tradeJudgement reads only trades the student starts and ranks 'behind' (:78) before 'attacker-gone' (:91). In #361's situation that is false teaching risk.
2. Repertoire advice is stripped. openingGenerator.ts:2246 strips 'easy to learn' as filler (V4), yet learnability advice is a real act of the reference coach (#195, #270, #330; the census counts about 250 such lines).
3. Rhetorical questions vs F05. All 7 questions in the slice are rhetorical and answered by the coach within one ply. F05 should be read as governing blocking asks only. The only question device in code is methodBeat.ts:145/309.
4. V8 vs material arithmetic. Is 'a piece is worth three pawns' a forbidden number?

Compliance finding (verified): 16 of 187 slice notes, and 679 of 7,477 in the whole corpus, keep the reference coach's first person (I/my/me). That breaks V1 and F0d. The perspective gate scans this corpus (src/data/perspectiveVoice.test.ts:69) but bans only we/our/us (:28) and explicitly allows I/my (:11-12). The notes are spoken in 'teach me X opening' and chat (S6/S7).

Caveats:
- The corpus is distilled. One video keeps only 37% of plies, the phase field mislabels (#219-#230 are tagged endgame with queens on), and no raw transcripts for these 8 videos are on disk.
- Another agent is editing this worktree live (learnBoardTeaching.ts and gemCrushLines.ts are modified). All file:line citations were re-verified in a final pass.
- Scratch outputs: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-chess-academy-pro/61fdf752-44c7-57cb-be1e-44a85a8d5754/scratchpad/slice.txt (the slice with chess.js context), stats.cjs, rhythm2.cjs, rhythm3.cjs.
rhythm:
Median 17 words per move across 187 notes. 20% are bare move statements of 8 words or fewer (castling, recaptures, opponent shuffles), and 11 notes run 40+ words.

Coverage: 82-100% of plies in 6 of 8 videos, so no move passes in silence (V11 holds). Routine plies get one clause that names the move; this is description, not teaching.

Opening density depends on the video type. Lecture games run 19-26 words a move in the opening (menus of named roads, reasons, warnings, line reputations). A casual game runs 11 words: name the system plus one clause.

Decision moments get 30-70+ words. Once a game is decided, the talk collapses to the move plus a material status (KID game: median 14 words while contested, 12 after the queen trade, with reasons almost gone). Under fire it grows (defence game: 18 words in the set-up, 23 under attack).

The unit is the THOUGHT, not the ply. 12 thoughts span 2-4 plies: the note ends on a dash and the next ply completes it, all in the two lecture videos. Our composer works per ply (thinkAloud.depthClauses).

On the opponent's ply he often starts the student's next decision (17 of 81 opponent-move notes): menus, 'choose carefully', a rhetorical 'what should you take?'.

Order inside a thought: their move and what it wants or changes → the student's answer → the reason → the tempting alternative and why it fails → sometimes the plan's next step. 18% of notes carry a but/rather/instead turn, and 13 name a rejected alternative.

All 7 questions are rhetorical and answered within one ply.

Across a game he threads ideas: arguments numbered over plies, a move rejected three times then played when its reason arrives, payoff callbacks, plan milestones.
